(p-3776) Surat an-Nahl

It is named after its mention of the words of Allah, the Exalted: "And your Lord inspired the bee" (an-nahl). This indicates that it is not far-fetched for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to inspire some of His special servants to extract from this Book sweet and healing benefits, by applying its words to the places of nobility, to the fruitful meanings, and to the lofty dispositions, together with acquiring virtuous character and following the path of purification and self-cleansing. This is the most complete means of recognising the virtues of the Qur'an and of grasping its objectives. This was said by al-Mahayimi.

Some of them said: Naming the surah thus is naming it after a matter of importance, so that the purpose it aims at may be noticed, like (al-Jumu'ah) for the importance of the weekly gathering and what results from it of public benefits, (al-Hadid) for its great benefits, (an-Nahl), (al-'Ankabut), and (an-Naml), so that one may take note of the small creatures with their wise crafts, and so on. A portion of the wisdom and secrets of the bee will come later at its verse in this surah.

It is Meccan. Ibn 'Abbas excepted its last part. From al-Sha'bi: except His saying, the Exalted, "And if you punish, then punish [with an equivalent]..." and its verses. And from al-Sha'bi: except His saying, the Exalted, "And those who emigrated for the cause of Allah..." and its verses. Its verses number one hundred and twenty-eight.

From Qatadah: it is called the Surah of Blessings, because Allah enumerates in it the blessings upon His servants.

(p-3777) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Discussion on the interpretation of His saying, the Exalted:

[1] "The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it. Exalted is He above what they associate with Him."

"The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it. Exalted is He above what they associate with Him." It has been established in more than one verse that the polytheists used to seek to hasten what they were promised of the Hour or of their destruction, as happened on the Day of Badr, mocking and denying the promise. So it was said to them: "The command of Allah has come," meaning: what you are threatened with, of what has been mentioned. The expression of it as "the command of Allah" is for magnification and awe, and to indicate that its realisation in itself and its coming is bound to His executed judgment and His overpowering decree. Its "coming" is an expression for its nearness and approach, in the manner of presenting what is expected as already in the category of what has occurred, or it refers to the coming of its near beginnings, in the manner of attributing the state of causes to their effects. The verse is like His saying, the Exalted: "The reckoning of people has drawn near to them, while they are heedless, turning away" [al-Anbiya: 1], and His saying: "The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split" [al-Qamar: 1], and His saying: "They ask you to hasten the punishment, and had there not been a specified term, the punishment would have come to them. And it will surely come upon them suddenly while they do not perceive" [al-'Ankabut: 53]. Then He, the Exalted, declared Himself free of their associating others with Him, and their worship alongside Him of what is other than Him, of idols and equals, which led them to mockery and obstinacy, and to their belief that these would be their intercessors when the appointed promise came.

The commentary on His words, may He be exalted:

[2] ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit by His command, upon whomever of His servants He wills, [saying]: "Warn that there is no god but Me, so fear Me."﴾

﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit by His command, upon whomever of His servants He wills, [saying]: "Warn that there is no god but Me, so fear Me."﴾ (p-3778) This is a response to their deeming prophethood improbable, [showing] that it is a practice (sunnah) of His, exalted is He. For this reason He used the form of the future tense, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿He casts the Spirit by His command upon whomever of His servants He wills﴾ [Ghafir: 15], and His words, exalted is He: ﴿God chooses messengers from among the angels and from among mankind﴾ [al-Hajj: 75]. The Spirit is the revelation, of which the Qur'an is a part, by His words, exalted is He: ﴿And thus We have revealed to you a Spirit from Our command. You did not know what the Scripture was, nor what faith was, but We made it a light by which We guide whomever of Our servants We will﴾ [al-Shura: 52]. Referring to it as "the Spirit" is in the manner of metaphor (isti'arah), for it gives life to hearts that are dead through ignorance. And: ﴿from His command﴾ is either an explanation of "the Spirit," or a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to it, or a qualifier (sifah), or it is connected to (yunazzilu) ["He sends down"], and [the particle] "min" here indicates causation (lil-sababiyyah). And: ﴿that warn﴾ (an andhiru) is a substitute (badal) for "the Spirit." That is: inform them of monotheism and piety. So His words ﴿so fear Me﴾ are part of what is to be conveyed in the warning. Or it is an address to those who were hastening [the punishment], by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), and the fa' is explanatory (fa' fasihah), meaning: if His practice is that, then fear Me, by avoiding what contradicts it of associating partners (shirk) and its branches, such as hastening [the punishment].

Al-Zamakhshari said: Then He indicated His oneness and that there is no god but Him, by what has been mentioned, of what no one other than Him is able to do, namely the creation of the heavens and the earth, the creation of man and what suits him, and what he cannot do without of the creation of livestock for his eating and riding, the carrying of his loads and all his other needs, and the creation of the kinds of creatures that they do not know. One like this is exalted above having anything associated with Him, by His words, glorified is He:

(p-3779)

The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, exalted is He:

[3-6] ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in truth; exalted is He above what they associate with Him.﴾ ﴿He created man from a drop of fluid, and then he is an open adversary.﴾ [al-Nahl: 4] ﴿And the cattle — He created them for you; in them is warmth and benefits, and from them you eat.﴾ [al-Nahl: 5] ﴿And for you in them is beauty when you bring them home at dusk and when you drive them out to pasture.﴾ [al-Nahl: 6]

﴿He created the heavens and the earth in truth﴾, i.e., with wisdom, as has preceded: ﴿exalted is He above what they associate with Him.﴾ ﴿He created man from a drop of fluid﴾ [al-Nahl: 4], i.e., a humble, weak thing; ﴿and then he is﴾ [al-Nahl: 4], after its completion, a human being: ﴿an open adversary﴾ [al-Nahl: 4], i.e., one who disputes with his Creator and argues, denying His oneness and warring against His messengers. He was only created to be a servant, not an opponent.

﴿And the cattle — He created them for you﴾ [al-Nahl: 5], i.e., for your welfare, and they are the eight pairs detailed in Surat al-An'am.

al-Zamakhshari said: The term is most often applied to camels.

﴿In them is warmth﴾ [al-Nahl: 5], i.e., that which gives warmth, that is, that by which one is warmed from wool, fur or hair, which protects from the cold. ﴿And benefits﴾ [al-Nahl: 5], i.e., from their offspring, their milk and riding their backs. ﴿And from them you eat﴾ [al-Nahl: 5]. ﴿And for you in them is beauty﴾ [al-Nahl: 6], i.e., adornment: ﴿when you bring them home﴾ [al-Nahl: 6], i.e., you return them from their pastures to their resting place (murah, with a dammed mim), which is their shelter in the dwellings of their people in the evening; ﴿and when you drive them out﴾ [al-Nahl: 6], i.e., you release them in the morning to the pastures.

al-Zamakhshari said: God has bestowed favour through the beauty they lend as He has through the benefit derived from them, for that is among the aims of livestock owners, indeed among its greatest. When the herdsmen bring them home in the evening and drive them out in the morning, they adorn the courtyards by their bringing home and their driving out, and their bleating and lowing resound within them; they bring comfort to their people, delight their owners, make them splendid in the eyes of onlookers, and win them standing and honour among people. Compare: ﴿That you may ride them and as adornment﴾ [al-Nahl: 8], ﴿It covers your private parts and is an adornment﴾ [al-A'raf: 26].

(p-3780) If you say: Why was bringing home mentioned before driving out? I say: Because the beauty is more apparent in bringing home, when they come back full-bellied, with udders swollen, and then take shelter in their enclosures with their people. End of quotation.

Then he pointed to a comprehensive benefit combining need and adornment, and said:

**The commentary on His words, exalted is He:**

[7-8] ﴿And He carries your loads to a land you could not have reached except with great hardship to yourselves. Surely your Lord is Most Kind, Most Merciful. And [He created] horses, mules and donkeys for you to ride and as adornment. And He creates what you do not know.﴾ [al-Nahl: 8].

﴿And He carries your loads﴾, meaning your burdens. ﴿To a land you could not have reached except with great hardship to yourselves﴾. The word *shiqq* (ش) is read with a kasra and with a fatha on the shin; these are two recitations, and they are two dialects with the same meaning, *al-mashaqqah* (hardship). The meaning is: you could not have reached it by your own selves except with effort and hardship, let alone carrying your loads on your backs. ﴿Surely your Lord is Most Kind, Most Merciful﴾, meaning in that He subjected them for your benefit.

Then He pointed to what is more complete in removing hardship and providing adornment, saying:

﴿And [He created] horses, mules and donkeys﴾ is coordinated with *al-an'am* (the grazing animals). ﴿For you to ride and as adornment﴾: the phrase *li-tarkabuhā* (for you to ride them) is taken as the object of the verb governing it by the coordination of position (*'atf mahall*), so *zīnatan* is either an object of purpose (*maf'ūl lahu*) or a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) of an omitted verb, meaning: "and you adorn yourselves with them as an adornment." Or it is a verbal noun standing in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) referring to the subject of *tarkabūhā* or to its object, meaning: "adorning yourselves with them" or "adorned with them." The secret of stating the particle *li-* (for) with the first item coordinated, but not with the second, is to indicate that the principal intended purpose among these categories is riding. As for adorning oneself with them, it is a secondary matter, not intended for its own sake in the way riding is. Thus the important intended purpose was joined with the particle *li-*, which expresses causation, to alert that it is the more important of the two aims and the stronger of the two causes. The adornment was left without the particle to signal that it is subordinate to, or less than, riding. And God knows best. Thus [says] *al-Intisaf*.

**A caution:**

Those who argue for the prohibition of eating horse meat have used this verse as evidence, saying that the causation by riding indicates that they were created for this benefit alone and not for anything else. They said: this is supported by the mention of these three kinds separately and their removal from the category of the grazing animals, which implies that their ruling is uniform regarding the prohibition of eating. They also said: if eating horses were permitted, then mentioning it and granting favour through it would have been more fitting than mentioning riding, because it is of greater benefit than riding.

Those who permit eating them responded that there is no proof in the causation by riding, because mentioning the most common of their benefits does not exclude others. We do not accept that eating is of greater benefit than riding so that it should be mentioned first and its mention should precede the mention of riding. Furthermore, if this verse indicated the prohibition of horses, it would indicate the prohibition of domestic donkeys, and then there would be no need to renew their prohibition on the day of Khaybar. We have already stated that this surah is Meccan.

The conclusion is that the sound evidences have shown the permissibility of eating horse meat. Even if we grant that this verse is a basis for those who argue for prohibition, the established pure Sunnah would remove this possibility and repel this inference. Hadiths have been transmitted concerning the permissibility of eating horse meat, among them what is in the two *Sahihs* and others, from the hadith of Asma, who said: "We slaughtered a horse during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and we ate it." Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sound, al-Nasa'i and others transmitted from Jabir, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) fed us the meat of horses and forbade us the meat of domestic donkeys." Abu Dawud transmitted something similar. It is also established in the two *Sahihs* from the hadith of Jabir, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade the meat of domestic donkeys and permitted horses."

As for what Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and others transmitted from the hadith of Khalid ibn al-Walid, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade eating every animal with fangs from the beasts of prey, and the meat of horses, mules and donkeys." Its chain includes Salih ibn Yahya, about whom there is criticism. Even if its authenticity were assumed, it would not be strong enough to oppose the hadiths of permissibility. Moreover, it is possible that it preceded the day of Khaybar, in which case it has been abrogated. Thus [says] *Fath al-Bayan*.

In *al-Iklil*: the Malikis took from the aforementioned juxtaposition a rebuttal of the Hanafis in their claim that zakat is obligatory on horses. That is, on horses.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And He creates what you do not know﴾, meaning among the created things in deserts and seas. The form of the present tense (*yakhluqu*) indicates renewal and continuity, or it serves to bring the image to mind.

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[9] ﴿And upon Allah is the direction of the way, and among them is a deviating one. And had He willed, He would have guided you all.﴾

Regarding this verse, there are several benefits:

The first: Ibn Kathir said: When He, exalted is He, mentioned among the animals those by which one travels along the sensory paths, He drew attention to the meaningful, religious paths. The Qur'an often moves from sensory matters to meaningful, religious matters, as in His saying: ﴿And take provision, for the best provision is piety﴾ [al-Baqarah: 197], and His saying: ﴿O children of Adam, We have sent down to you clothing to conceal your private parts and as adornment; but the clothing of piety—that is best﴾ [al-A'raf: 26].

When He, exalted is He, mentioned in this surah the animals of the livestock and others, which they ride and by which they reach a need within their breasts, and which carry their burdens to distant lands and places and arduous journeys, He began to mention the paths which people take to Him. He made clear that the true ones among them lead to Him, so He said: ﴿And upon Allah is the direction of the way﴾, like His saying: ﴿And that this is My path, [being] straight, so follow it. And do not follow [other] paths, for they will separate you from His way﴾ [al-An'am: 153], and He said: ﴿This is a path [leading] to Me, straight﴾ [al-Hijr: 41]. End quote. And His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, upon Us is guidance﴾ [al-Layl: 12].

The second: Abu al-Su'ud said: "al-qasd" (the direction) is a verbal noun used in the sense of the active participle. It is said: a sabil qasd and qasid, meaning straight. It is either in the manner of metaphor, or in the manner of attributing the state of its traveler to it, as if it intends the direction which the traveler aims at and does not deviate from. That is: it is incumbent upon Him, glorified and exalted is He, by the necessity of His mercy and His binding promise, to make clear the straight path which leads whoever travels it to the truth, which is monotheism, by establishing the proofs, sending the messengers, and sending down the books to call people to it. Or it is a verbal noun in the sense of setting upright and making balanced, as Abu al-Baqa' said. That is: upon Him, mighty and majestic, is its straightening and its balancing, that is, making it such that its traveler reaches the truth—but not after it had been deviating from it in its own nature; rather, its origination from the beginning is thus, in the manner of (Glory be to He who made the gnat small and made the elephant great). Its reality returns to what was mentioned of establishing the proofs. He did so when He originated these wonders, each one of which is a clear road guided by its beacon, and a sign illuminated by its fire, and He sent messengers as bringers of glad tidings and warners, and sent down upon them books, among which is this revelation that speaks the reality of the truth, that examines every secret, subtle or grand, that guides to the way of reasoning by those proofs which lead to the landmarks of guidance, which rescue from the wastelands of error and the abysses of perdition.

The third: The pronoun in ﴿and among them is a deviating one﴾ refers to the "sabil" (way), for it is feminine. That is: some of the way is inclined away from the truth, deviating from it, not leading its traveler to it. These are the paths of error whose number is almost uncountable, all of which are included under the "deviating one," as in His saying: ﴿And that this is My path, [being] straight, so follow it. And do not follow [other] paths, for they will separate you from His way﴾ [al-An'am: 153].

Abu al-Su'ud said, after what has preceded: That is, upon Allah, exalted is He, is the clarifying of the straight path that leads to the truth and its straightening, by what has been mentioned of establishing the proofs, so that people may travel it by their own choice and reach the goal. This is the guidance that is explained as indicating what leads to the sought objective, not the guidance that necessarily entails being guided absolutely. For that is not something binding upon Allah, exalted is He—neither by His essence nor by His mercy; rather, it would disrupt His wisdom, since it would require equating the doer of good and the doer of evil, and the obedient and the disobedient, according to their readiness. And to this He alluded by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And had He willed, He would have guided you all﴾, that is: had He willed to guide you to what has been mentioned of monotheism, with a guidance that absolutely leads you to it, necessarily entailing that you all be guided, He would have done so. But He did not will it, because His will follows wisdom, which calls for it. And there is no wisdom in that will, since that upon which the orbit of obligation revolves, and to which reward and punishment are attached, is only choice, upon which the deeds are based, and by which the recompense is tied.

Since the most noble of the bodies of the lower world, after animals, is plants, and what passed of the livestock was followed by the cattle and beasts, by which His oneness, exalted is He, is inferred, He mentioned the wonders of the states of plants, for the same wisdom. So He, glorified is He, said:

**The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:**

[10–11] ﴿It is He who sends down water from the sky; from it is drink, and from it are trees, in which you pasture your livestock.﴾ ﴿He causes to grow for you thereby the crops, the olives, the date palms, the grapes, and of all the fruits. Indeed in that is a sign for a people who give thought.﴾ [al-Nahl: 11].

﴿It is He who sends down from the sky﴾, meaning the clouds, ﴿water; from it is drink﴾, which quenches the heat of thirst. ﴿And from it are trees﴾, meaning from it there comes forth trees. What is intended thereby is that which grows from the earth, whether it has a trunk or not. ﴿In which you pasture﴾, meaning you graze your livestock.

﴿He causes to grow﴾ [al-Nahl: 11], meaning God, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿for you thereby the crops﴾ [al-Nahl: 11], meaning that in which is the sustenance of man; ﴿the olives﴾ [al-Nahl: 11], meaning that in which is its condiment; ﴿the date palms and the grapes﴾ [al-Nahl: 11], meaning those in which, in addition to that, is greater enjoyment and pleasure; ﴿and of all the fruits﴾ [al-Nahl: 11], meaning He brings them forth with this one water, despite the difference in their kinds, their tastes, their colours and their scents. For this reason He said: ﴿Indeed in that﴾ [al-Nahl: 11], meaning in the sending down and the causing to grow of what was detailed, ﴿is a sign for a people who give thought﴾ [al-Nahl: 11], meaning a proof and an argument for His oneness, Exalted is He. As He, Glorified is He, said: ﴿Is He not better who created the heavens and the earth and sent down for you water from the sky, whereby We caused to grow gardens of delightful beauty, which you could not have caused their trees to grow? Is there a god with God? Nay, but they are a people who ascribe equals [to Him]﴾ [al-Naml: 60].

Abu al-Su'ud said: Its origin is from al-Razi, in explaining how what he mentioned is a proof. For whoever reflects on the fact that the seed or the pit falls into the earth, and moisture reaches it and penetrates it, so that its lower part splits and from it roots emerge spreading into the depths of the earth, and its upper part splits, even though it is inverted in its falling, and from it a stem emerges and grows, and from it come forth leaves, blossoms, grains and fruits, comprising bodies of differing shapes, colours, properties and natures, and a seed capable of producing its like in the same pattern, without end, (p-3786) with the matter being the same and the influence of the lower natures and the higher influences being equal in relation to all of them; he knows that whoever has these acts and effects cannot be resembled by anything in any of the attributes of perfection, let alone that the lowest of things should share with Him in His most distinctive attribute, which is divinity and the deserving of worship. Exalted is He far above that, a great exaltation. And since the pursuit of this method required the arrangement of intellectual premises, the noble verse concluded with reflection. End of quotation. And His saying, Exalted is He:

And His saying, Exalted is He:

The discussion concerning His words, exalted is He:

[12] ﴿And He subjected to you the night and the day, and the sun and the moon, and the stars are subjected by His command. Indeed in that are signs for a people who use their intellect.﴾

﴿And He subjected to you the night and the day﴾, i.e., for your sleep and your livelihood, and for the setting and ripening of fruits. ﴿And the sun and the moon﴾ [He subjected] for the regulation of the created things whose well-being is bound to them. ﴿And the stars﴾ [He subjected] so that they may be guided by them in the darknesses of land and sea. His words, exalted is He, ﴿subjected by His command﴾ are a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to all of them, in the sense of "He made them subjected"; because subjection (al-taskhīr) includes the meaning of "making" (al-ja'l), so it is correct, as a form of abstraction (tajrīd). Or [it is correct] on the basis that the subjection is a particular benefit for them.

Its meaning, then, is: your benefit, while they are subjected to that for which they were created, of what is a means to your benefit. Thus (sakhkhara) carries the meaning of (nafa'a, "benefited"), by way of metaphor (isti'āra) or the sent metonymy (al-majāz al-mursal), because benefit is among the necessary consequences of subjection. Or [it is correct] on the basis that (musakhkharāt, "subjected") is a mīmī verbal noun (maṣdar mīmī), in the accusative as an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq). [The sense is] "He subjected them in a state of subjection," like "I struck him with strikes" (ḍarabtuhu ḍarabāt). Or His words ﴿subjected by His command﴾ may be taken to mean "continuously subjected to the subjection by His originating command (amr al-ījād)," because bringing into existence does not indicate continuity.

It was also read with the accusative for "the night and the day" alone, and the nominative for what follows them, as an inchoative and predicate (mubtada' and khabar). And it was read: ﴿and the stars are subjected﴾ with the nominative as an inchoative and predicate, and what precedes it in the accusative. ﴿Indeed in that﴾, i.e., the subjection of what has been mentioned, ﴿are signs for a people who use their intellect.﴾

When He, exalted is He, drew attention to the landmarks of the heavens, He drew attention to what He created on the earth of wondrous matters and diverse things, from animals, minerals, plants and inanimate objects, in their varying colours and forms, and the benefits and properties that are in them, by His words, glorified is He:

The discussion of the Exalted's saying:

[13] ﴿And what He has created for you on the earth of various colors. Indeed in that is a sign for a people who are mindful.﴾

﴿And what He has created﴾ is conjoined with His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and the stars﴾ [an-Nahl: 12], in both the nominative and accusative cases, on the basis that it is an object of (ja'ala, "He made"), meaning: and what He created ﴿for you on the earth﴾, that is, of animals and plants, ﴿of various colors. Indeed in that is a sign for a people who are mindful.﴾

Then the Exalted, bestowing favor, drew attention to His subjecting the sea and enumerating the blessings in it, following His favor through the blessings of the land, by His saying:

On the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[14] ﴿It is He who subjected the sea, that you may eat from it fresh flesh, and extract from it ornaments which you wear; and you see the ships ploughing through it, that you may seek of His bounty, and perhaps you will be grateful.﴾

﴿It is He who subjected the sea, that you may eat from it fresh flesh﴾ — this is fish.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He described it as fresh because decay quickly sets in upon it, so one hastens to eat it for fear of its spoiling.

Al-Nasir said: It is as if this were an instruction regarding its consumption and a guidance that it should not be taken except when fresh. The physicians say: consuming it after its freshness has gone is among the most harmful things. And God knows best. End of quote.

(p-3788) Al-Shihab said: Thus it contains an incidental inclusion of a medical ruling. This does not contradict its being dried or eaten pickled, as has been supposed. End of quote.

I say: The more apparent wisdom in describing it as fresh is to draw attention to its goodness and delicacy, and to reflection upon the manifest power and wondrous craftsmanship of God, exalted is He, in His creation of it, in the manner in which the flesh of land animals varies, despite both sharing animality.

﴿And extract from it ornaments﴾ such as pearls and coral: ﴿which you wear﴾, i.e., your women wear them. The attribution is to you because they are part of you through association and dependence, and because they adorn themselves with them for your sake, so they are your adornment and clothing. Or the meaning of "you wear" is "you enjoy and take pleasure," by way of metaphor and figurative speech. If it were taken as a metonymy of the part, it would also be valid, i.e., your women wear them.

Al-Nasir said: How right Malik, may God be pleased with him, was, in making for the husband the authority to restrain his wife in matters of her property that are significant, and this is limited to what exceeds one third, for he has a right in it through her adornment. Behold the standing of men's share in women's wealth and in their adornment, to the point that he made the woman's share of her wealth and adornment an ornament for him. Thus he expressed his share in her wearing them by his wearing them, just as he expresses her share in the same way.

Al-Shihab said: If you say: the apparent wording should be "you unlock them" or "you adorn them with them," as in the saying:

"Its pebbles dismay the bejewelled maidens, so it touches the edge of the strung necklace."

and these are for women, not men. I say: As for the first, it is easy, for what is meant is its necessary consequence, i.e., you unlock them. As for the second, granting its acceptance: men enjoy the adornment of women, so it is as if they were wearing them. If it is not a case of predominance, then it is metaphorical, meaning: you make them a garment for your daughters and wives.

The reason for the deviation: women are commanded to veil and to conceal adornment from non-mahrams. So the explicit mention of this was concealed, so that the wording would be like the meaning. End of quote.

The author of Fath al-Bayan examined what they had estimated in the verse, saying: The apparent meaning of His words, ﴿you wear them﴾, is that it is permissible for men to wear pearls and coral, i.e., they make them an ornament for themselves just as it is permissible for women. There is no need for what a group of exegetes burdened themselves with in interpreting His words "you wear them" as "your women wear them," because they are part of you, or because they wear them for your sake. Nothing in the purified Shariah requires forbidding men from adorning themselves with pearls and coral, so long as they do not use them in a manner that is used only by women. For that is forbidden, and the Shariah has prohibited it on account of its being an imitation of women, not on account of its being an ornament of pearl or coral. End of quote.

Al-Suyuti said in al-Iklil: The verse is evidence for the permissibility of men wearing jewels and the like. Some have used it to argue that one who swears not to wear jewelry is in breach by wearing pearls, because He, exalted is He, named it "ornament" (ḥilyah). Some have also used it to argue that there is no zakat on women's ornaments. Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Ja'far that he was asked: Is there charity on women's ornaments? He said: No, they are as He said: ﴿ornaments which you wear﴾. End of quote.

He said in Fath al-Bayan: There is room for scrutiny in this argument. What should be relied upon is that the original state is freedom from zakat until evidence is found requiring it in some kind of wealth, whereupon it becomes obligatory. It has been related concerning gold and silver what is well known. No evidence has come concerning jewels, in their various kinds, that indicates the obligation of zakat upon them.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿and you see the ships﴾, i.e., the boats: ﴿ploughing through it﴾, i.e., running, plural of ﴿mākhirah﴾ in the sense of "jāriyah" (running). The root meaning of "al-makhr" is cleaving, because they cleave the water with their prows. ﴿That you may seek of His bounty﴾ is a conjunction with an omitted element, i.e., that you may benefit by that, ﴿and that you may seek of His bounty﴾, i.e., of the abundance of His provision, by riding them for trade. ﴿And perhaps you will be grateful﴾, i.e., that you may direct what He has bestowed upon you to that for which He created it.

(p-3790) Abu al-Su'ud said: Perhaps the singling out of this blessing for mention with gratitude is because in it is the crossing of a long distance, with heavy loads, in a short period, without exerting the means of travel, indeed without any movement at all, while being amid perils. The omission of placing the attainment of the sought-after between seeking and gratitude is to indicate that it is sufficiently understood without explicit mention, and that both occur together.

His words, exalted is He:

The discussion of the Almighty's words:

[15–16] ﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains, lest it shake with you, and rivers and roads, that you may be guided﴾ ﴿and landmarks; and by the star they are guided﴾ [al-Nahl: 16].

﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains﴾ meaning: stable mountains. ﴿Lest it shake with you﴾ meaning: lest it convulse. ﴿And rivers﴾ meaning: He placed in it rivers flowing from one place to another, as provision for the servants. ﴿And roads﴾ meaning: paths along which one travels from one land to another, even through the mountains, as the Exalted said: ﴿And We made in them broad roads as paths﴾ [al-Anbiya': 31]. ﴿That you may be guided﴾ meaning: by them to your destinations.

﴿And landmarks﴾ [al-Nahl: 16] meaning: signs by which travelers take their bearings from a mountain, a watering place, or a wind, on land and at sea, when they lose the way. ﴿And by the star they are guided﴾ [al-Nahl: 16] meaning: in darkness, on land and at sea.

The shift from the mode of address to the third person is an iltifat (turn of discourse). The fronting of ﴿bi-al-najm﴾ (by the star) is for the sake of the rhyme (fasilah), and the fronting of the pronoun is for emphasis. This is preferable to the claim of al-Zamakhshari that the fronting is for restriction to a people, namely the Quraysh, because they were people of journeys and travel; this is because the address in the preceding verses is general, so it should likewise be general in what follows.

Note:

In al-Iklil, he said: this verse is a basis for observing the stars to know the times, the qiblah, and the routes.

(p-3791)

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[17-18] ﴿Is He who creates like one who creates not? Will you not then remember?﴾ ﴿And if you should count the favor of Allah, you could not enumerate it. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ [An-Nahl: 18].

﴿Is He who creates﴾ i.e., everything, especially those great creations mentioned, and He is Allah, the One, the Unique: ﴿like one who creates not﴾ i.e., anything at all, and that is what they worship besides Him. This is a rebuke to the polytheists and a refutation of their associating partners with Him, by denying that what cannot create any of that, but rather can bring into existence only something of some kind, could be equal to Him or deserve to share in His worship.

Al-Zamakhshari (d. 538 AH) and his followers claimed that the requirement of the argument is that it be said: "Is one who creates not like one who creates?" Then they spoke about its secret. The discussion of that has already passed at His words, exalted is He: ﴿And the male is not like the female﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 36], so it is renewed in memory: ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ i.e., so that you may recognize the corruption of that, for its clarity requires nothing beyond remembrance.

Then He, glorified and exalted, drew attention to the abundance of His blessings upon them and His bounty beyond counting, indicating that the due of His worship is beyond capacity, by His words, exalted is He: ﴿And if you should count the favor of Allah, you could not enumerate it﴾ [An-Nahl: 18] i.e., you cannot fix their number, nor can your capacity reach it, let alone that you could fulfill the duty of thanking Him for them: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [An-Nahl: 18] i.e., in that He overlooks the shortcoming in rendering thanks for them, does not cut them off from you because of your negligence, and does not hasten punishment upon you for your ingratitude. Thus said al-Zamakhshari.

Ibn Jarir noted that His forgiveness and mercy toward them are when they repent and turn back. i.e., He overlooks their shortcoming in giving true thanks, and does not punish them after their repentance and their turning back to His obedience.

A subtle point:

Abu al-Su'ud said: The apparent arrangement would have been to place this verse directly after the enumerated blessings, as a completion of them, in the manner of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And He creates what you do not know﴾ [An-Nahl: 8]. Perhaps the separation between them by His words ﴿Is He who creates﴾ is for the sake of hastening to establish the proof and cast the stone, following the detailing of the acts that He detailed, which are the evidences of His oneness.

The discourse on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[19–21] ﴿And Allah knows what you conceal and what you disclose.﴾ ﴿And those they invoke besides Allah create nothing, and they are themselves created.﴾ [An-Nahl: 20] ﴿They are dead, not living; and they do not perceive when they will be resurrected.﴾ [An-Nahl: 21]

﴿And Allah knows what you conceal and what you disclose﴾, i.e., of your deeds, and He will recompense you for it.

﴿And those they invoke besides Allah create nothing, and they are themselves created﴾ [An-Nahl: 20], i.e., how then can they deserve divinity (al-uluhiyyah, godhood), when the most distinctive of its attributes has been negated from them? For they are essences in need of being brought into existence. Or the meaning is: people create them by carving and shaping, and they are not able to do the like of that, so they are more powerless than their worshippers, as the Friend (al-Khalil), peace be upon him, said: ﴿Do you worship what you carve? And Allah created you and what you make﴾ [As-Saffat: 95–96].

Then He emphasized this by ascribing to them what contradicts divinity, saying:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 16, verses 22–23:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[22–23] ﴿Your God is one God. As for those who do not believe in the Hereafter, their hearts are denying, and they are arrogant.﴾ ﴿Undoubtedly, Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal. Indeed, He does not like the arrogant.﴾ [al-Nahl: 22–23].

﴿Your God is one God﴾ is a declaration of the claim and a clear statement of the conclusion, after establishing the proof, as Abu al-Su'ud has conveyed. ﴿As for those who do not believe in the Hereafter, their hearts are denying﴾, meaning: they deny His oneness, rejecting it, as He informed about them, marveling at it in His saying: ﴿Has he made the gods one God? Indeed, this is a strange thing!﴾ [Sad: 5]. And the Exalted said: ﴿And when Allah alone is mentioned, the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter shrink with aversion, but when those other than Him are mentioned, behold, they rejoice﴾ [al-Zumar: 45]. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they are arrogant﴾, meaning: arrogant toward His worship, exalted is He.

﴿Undoubtedly [la jaram]﴾ [al-Nahl: 23], meaning: truly. ﴿Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal. Indeed, He does not like the arrogant﴾ [al-Nahl: 23], meaning: those arrogant toward monotheism, who are the polytheists; or arrogant toward the truth absolutely, so it encompasses these as well. This is like the Exalted's saying: ﴿Indeed, those who are arrogant about worshipping Me will enter Hell, humiliated﴾ [Ghafir: 60].

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 16, verses 24–25:**

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[24–25] ﴿When it is said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?" they say, "Fables of the ancients."﴾ ﴿That they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection, and some of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge. Unquestionably, evil is what they bear.﴾ [al-Nahl: 25].

﴿When it is said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?" they say, "Fables of the ancients."﴾ That is: He has sent down nothing. Rather, what is recited to us is only the tales of the ancients, which he (Muhammad ﷺ) drew from them. As He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they say, "Fables of the ancients, which he has had written down, so they are dictated to him morning and evening."﴾ [al-Furqan: 5].

﴿That they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection, and some of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge﴾ [al-Nahl: 25]. That is: they said that so that they would bear their own particular burdens, which are the burdens of their own misguidance, and some of the burdens of those whom they misled, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They will surely bear their burdens and burdens along with their burdens, and they will surely be questioned on the Day of Resurrection about what they used to invent.﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 13]. So the lam in His saying ﴿li-yahmilu﴾ [al-Nahl: 25] is the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah), since what is mentioned follows from their action. It is not a lam of motive, either metaphorically or literally, in the sense that its occurrence from them was decreed in order that they would bear. It has been said that it is a lam of causation, and that it is a decisive imperative lam (lam al-amr al-jazimah). The meaning is: that is necessarily binding upon them. The sentence is then complete at His saying ﴿fables of the ancients﴾, as is stated in (al-'Inayah).

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿without knowledge﴾ [al-Nahl: 25], al-Zamakhshari said: it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object: that is, of those who do not know that they are astray. He described those whom they misled as astray and as bearing the burden, even though he did not know, because it was incumbent upon him to investigate and to consider with his intellect until he distinguished between the truthful and the falsehood. So his ignorance does not excuse him. ﴿Unquestionably, evil is what they bear﴾ [al-Nahl: 25]. That is: unquestionably, evil is what they carry. In it is a warning and a threat.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 16, verse 26:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[26] ﴿Those before them had already schemed, so Allah came at their structures from their foundations, and the roof fell down on them from above them, and the punishment came to them from where they did not perceive.﴾

﴿Those before them had already schemed﴾ i.e., against their prophets. ﴿So Allah came at their structures from their foundations, and the roof fell down on them from above them﴾ i.e., He uprooted their structures from their bases and their foundations, so He caused it to collapse upon them until He destroyed them. The "coming" (al-ityan) is used figuratively for "destruction" (al-ihlak), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So Allah came at them from where they did not expect﴾ [al-Hashr: 2]. It is said: "So-and-so was come upon from his place of safety," meaning ruin came to him from the direction of his security. And "time came upon him" (ata 'alayhi al-dahr) means it destroyed him and annihilated him. From this comes al-utu', which is death and affliction. It is said: "Utu' came upon so-and-so," meaning death or affliction befell him. It has also been permitted that the verse intends the literal sense of their destruction, as related about the people of Lot and Salih, peace be upon them both, as was mentioned earlier. Or its meaning is figurative, by way of illustration (tamthil), to nullify what they had devised of demolishing His religion. The state of those schemers, in their arranging of plots to bring down the messengers, peace be upon them, is likened to His nullifying those stratagems and making them the causes of their destruction, to the state of a people who built a structure and supported it with pillars. Then that came upon them from the direction of its pillars, as those were weakened and the roof fell on them, and they perished. The aspect of resemblance is that what they considered the cause of their survival became the cause of their annihilation and extinction, like their saying: "Whoever digs a pit for his brother falls into it headlong." His saying ﴿from above them﴾ is connected to (kharra). The "min" here indicates the starting point, or it is connected to an omitted element, as a confirmatory circumstantial clause (hal) from (al-saqf). It has been said that it is not for emphasis, because the Arabs say: "A roof collapsed on us, and a wall fell on us," when it has collapsed on his property even if it did not fall directly on him. ﴿And the punishment came to them﴾ i.e., the destruction and ruin. ﴿From where they did not perceive﴾ i.e., where they did not expect.

(p-3796)

The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, the Exalted:

[27] ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection He will disgrace them and say, "Where are My partners, about whom you used to oppose [the believers]?" Those who were given knowledge will say, "Indeed, disgrace and misfortune this Day are upon the disbelievers."﴾

﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection He will disgrace them﴾ i.e., He will humiliate them and abase them with the punishment of disgrace, due to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Our Lord, indeed whomever You admit to the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him﴾ [Al-Imran: 192]. ﴿And say, "Where are My partners, about whom you used to oppose [the believers]?"﴾ i.e., you used to be hostile to and dispute with the believers concerning them. In this there is rebuke and reproach by speech, and mockery of them, since He attributed the partners to Himself on the slightest connection, in accordance with their own claim, along with humiliation through the action implied by His saying, ﴿He will disgrace them﴾. That is: what is wrong with them that they do not come to you to defend you? For they used to say: "If what you say is true, then the idols will intercede for us." So this is like His saying: ﴿Where are your partners whom you used to claim?﴾ [Al-An'am: 22]. It was also said: this is related from the polytheists as an additional reproach against them. ﴿Those who were given knowledge﴾, and they are the prophets or the scholars, who used to call them to the truth and whom they opposed, will say: ﴿Indeed, disgrace and misfortune this Day﴾, i.e., the disgrace and the punishment, ﴿are upon the disbelievers﴾, i.e., those who associated others with Allah, the Exalted, that which neither harms them nor benefits them. And His saying, ﴿Those who were given knowledge﴾, was only said as a means of gloating over them, adding humiliation through rebuke by speech, affirming what they used to be admonished with, and confirming what they had been threatened with.

(p-3797) The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[28-29] ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves. Then they will offer submission, [saying], "We did not do any evil." Yes, indeed Allah is Knowing of what you used to do.﴾ ﴿So enter the gates of Hell, to abide therein. And wretched is the abode of the arrogant.﴾ [al-Nahl: 29].

﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves. Then they will offer submission, [saying], "We did not do any evil." Yes, indeed Allah is Knowing of what you used to do.﴾ ﴿So enter the gates of Hell, to abide therein. And wretched is the abode of the arrogant.﴾ [al-Nahl: 29] This is an report about the state of the polytheists who wrong themselves by altering the fitrah (natural disposition) of Allah, at the time of their dying, when the angels come to them to seize their souls. [It describes] that they "offer submission" (ألقوا السلم, al-salam), meaning they yield, make peace, and abandon opposition. The shift to the past tense form (al-madi) is to indicate the certainty of its occurrence. The original meaning of "ilqa'" (casting) is applied to bodies, but here it is used for showing submission, to convey the extent of their humility and abasement. This is treated as like an object cast before the feet of the overpowering conqueror, by way of metaphor.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"We did not do any evil"﴾ is in the accusative case (mansub) governed by a concealed verb, as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: saying that. Or it is an explanation (tafsir) of "the submission" (السلم) that they offered, because it has the meaning of "saying," as evidenced by the other verse: ﴿Then they will cast to them the saying﴾ [al-Nahl: 86], just as they will say on the Day of Return: ﴿"By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists"﴾ [al-An'am: 23], ﴿On the Day when Allah resurrects them all and they swear to Him as they swear to you﴾ [al-Mujadila: 18].

Then Allah, exalted is He, informed that the angels respond to them with His saying: ﴿"Yes, indeed Allah is Knowing of what you used to do."﴾ That is, denial and lying against themselves are of no benefit. ﴿"So enter the gates of Hell, to abide therein"﴾ [al-Nahl: 29], that is, your eternal abiding being decreed.

Ibn Kathir said: They enter Hell from the day of their death with their souls, and its heat and scorching winds reach their bodies in their graves. (p-3798) When the Day of Resurrection comes, their souls are returned into their bodies, and they abide forever in the Fire of Hell, ﴿for it will not be decreed for them so that they die, nor will its punishment be lightened for them﴾ [Fatir: 36], as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿The Fire, they are exposed to it morning and evening, and on the day the Hour is established: "Admit the people of Pharaoh to the severest punishment."﴾ [Ghafir: 46]. And His saying: ﴿"And wretched is the abode of the arrogant"﴾ [al-Nahl: 29], that is, wretched is the resting place and dwelling for one who was arrogant toward the signs of Allah and toward following His messengers. He mentioned them by the description of arrogance, to indicate that this is the cause of their remaining therein. Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 16, verse 30:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[30] ﴿And it will be said to those who were mindful of God, "What has your Lord sent down?" They will say, "Good." For those who did good in this world there is good, and the abode of the Hereafter is better. And excellent indeed is the abode of the God-fearing.﴾

﴿And it will be said to those who were mindful of God﴾, and they are the believers: ﴿"What has your Lord sent down?" They will say, "Good."﴾ That is: He sent down good, that is, mercy and blessing for whoever follows it and believes in it. Then He, glory be to Him, informed of what He promised His servants by His words: ﴿For those who did good in this world there is good, and the abode of the Hereafter is better.﴾ That is: for whoever made his deeds good, a reward in this world for their goodness, and for them in the Hereafter is what is better than it. So His words ﴿in this world﴾ are connected to ﴿good﴾ just as they are connected to ﴿did good﴾. Al-Shihab said: The "good" in this world is victory, good conduct, and other than that. This verse is like His words, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely reward them with their best deeds﴾ [al-Nahl: 97], and His words: ﴿So God gave them the reward of this world and the good reward of the Hereafter﴾ [Al 'Imran: 148], and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And what is with God is better for the righteous﴾ [Al 'Imran: 198], and He said: ﴿But the Hereafter is better and more enduring﴾ [al-A'la: 17]. Then He, exalted is He, described the abode of the Hereafter by His words: ﴿And excellent indeed is the abode of the God-fearing.﴾

The discussion of the words of His exalted saying:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 16, verse 35–36 (part 1 of 2):

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[35-36] ﴿And those who associated others with Allah said: "Had Allah willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him—neither we nor our fathers—nor would we have prohibited anything without Him." Likewise did those before them act. So is there upon the messengers except clear conveyance?﴾ ﴿And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger, [saying], "Worship Allah and avoid the Taghut (false deities, every object of worship besides Allah)." Among them were those whom Allah guided, and among them were those upon whom error was made inevitable. So travel through the earth and observe how was the end of the deniers.﴾ [An-Nahl: 36].

﴿And those who associated others with Allah said: "Had Allah willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him—neither we nor our fathers—nor would we have prohibited anything without Him."﴾ Likewise did those before them act. So is there upon the messengers except clear conveyance?﴾ ﴿And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger, [saying], "Worship Allah and avoid the Taghut."﴾ Among them were those whom Allah guided, and among them were those upon whom error was made inevitable. So travel through the earth and observe how was the end of the deniers.﴾ [An-Nahl: 36]

He, exalted is He, informs of the deception of the polytheists regarding what they were in, and their excusing themselves from it by arguing with predestination (al-qadar), as a denial of the Messenger, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, and a slander against the message. Their saying is: ﴿Had Allah willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him—neither we nor our fathers—nor would we have prohibited anything without Him,﴾ meaning: the baheera, the sa'iba, the wasila and other things they had invented and devised from their own inclinations, for which Allah had sent down no authority. Then He, exalted is He, informed of their resemblance to those who preceded them, by His saying: ﴿Likewise did those before them act,﴾ meaning: in associating others with Allah and prohibiting, adhering to a similar doubt.

Ibn Kathir said: The substance of their speech is that if Allah, exalted is He, were averse to what we did, He would have denounced it against us with punishment, and would not have empowered us to do it. Allah, exalted is He, replied to their doubts: ﴿So is there upon the messengers except clear conveyance?﴾ meaning: the matter is not as you claim, that He did not denounce it to you. Rather, He denounced it to you in the strongest terms, forbade it to you with the most emphatic prohibition, and sent into every nation—meaning, into every generation and group of people—a messenger. All of them called to the worship of Allah and forbade the worship of anything other than Him: ﴿Worship Allah and avoid the Taghut﴾ [An-Nahl: 36], which is whatever is worshipped besides Him, glorified is He. Thus He, exalted is He, continued to send messengers to the people with this, from the time shirk arose among the children of Adam, from the era of Noah, the first messenger to the people of the earth, until the time of the Seal of the Prophets, may the blessings of Allah be upon him and upon them all. The call of all of them is one, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We did not send before you any messenger except that We revealed to him that there is no deity except Me, so worship Me﴾ [Al-Anbiya: 25], and as He informed here in this verse. So how can any of the polytheists after this say: ﴿Had Allah willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him﴾?

His legislative will (al-mashi'a al-shar'iyya) regarding them is thus negated, because He forbade them from that through the tongues of His messengers. As for His existential will (al-mashi'a al-kawniyya), which is His enabling them to do so by decree, they have no proof in it—meaning, because it is among the secret of predestination which is forbidden to delve into. Then He, exalted is He, informed that He denounced them with punishment in this world, after the warning of the messengers, by His saying: ﴿Among them were those whom Allah guided﴾ [An-Nahl: 36], and the verse.

We have previously cited in Surah al-An'am what the scholars said concerning verses like this one. We shall also here cite what I read of Imam Ibn Taymiyya, may Allah have mercy on him, at the beginning of the second part of (Minhaj al-Sunna) concerning the verse, although a quotation from him has already preceded us. The verse is among the battlegrounds of understanding, so there is no harm in our clearing from its doubts the rust of misconceptions. He, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is a station in which souls much plunge. For many people, when they are commanded to do what is obligatory upon them, make excuses by predestination and say: "Until Allah decrees that," or "Until Allah empowers me to that," or "Until Allah decides that." Likewise, when they are forbidden from doing what Allah has prohibited, they say: "Allah decreed it upon me," and similar speech. Arguing by predestination is a false and refuted argument, by the agreement of every person of intellect and religion among all the worlds. One who argues with it does not accept such an argument from others when they use it to justify an injustice they commit against him and a neglect of the rights they owe him. Rather, he demands from them what is due to him and punishes them for their aggression against him. It is of the same kind as the doubts of the sophists which arise in the sciences; you know their corruption by necessity, though they often occur to many people, to the point that one may doubt his own existence and other self-evident matters. Likewise, this (doubt) occurs in actions, until one thinks it is a doubt against the establishment of truthfulness and obligatory justice, and so on, and the permissibility of lying and injustice, and so on. But the hearts know by necessity that this is a false doubt. For this reason, no one accepts it upon careful examination, and no one argues with it except when he lacks knowledge of the proof concerning what he has done. When he knows that what he has done is the good, is what he was commanded, and is what ought to be done, he does not argue by predestination. Likewise, when he knows that what he did not do is not obligatory upon him, or is not beneficial, or is not what he was commanded, he does not argue by predestination. Rather, when he follows his desire without knowledge, he argues by predestination. For this reason, when the polytheists said: ﴿Had Allah willed, we would not have associated anything with Him, nor would our fathers, nor would we have prohibited anything﴾ [Al-An'am: 148], Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do you have any knowledge that you could produce for us? You follow nothing but assumption, and you are only guessing﴾ [Al-An'am: 148], ﴿Say: "To Allah belongs the conclusive argument. So had He willed, He would have guided you all"﴾ [Al-An'am: 149]. These polytheists know by their natural disposition and their intellects that this argument is refuted and false. For if one of them wronged another, or took his property, or violated his wife, or killed his child, or persisted in injustice, and people forbade him from that, and he said: "Had Allah willed, I would not have done this," they would not accept this argument from him, nor would he accept it from others. One only argues with it to repel blame without any basis. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do you have any knowledge that you could produce for us?﴾ [Al-An'am: 148], meaning that this shirk and prohibition are from the command of Allah, and that it is a benefit that ought to be done. ﴿You follow nothing but assumption﴾ [Al-An'am: 148], for you have no knowledge of that; you only assume it as a mere assumption. ﴿And you are only guessing﴾ [Al-An'am: 148], and fabricating. Your reliance in reality is your assumption and your guessing; your reliance in reality is not that Allah willed that and decreed it. For mere will and predestination are not a basis for anyone in an action, nor a proof of one person against another, nor an excuse for anyone, since all people share in predestination. If this were a proof and a basis, there would be no distinction between the just and the unjust, the truthful and the liar, the knowing and the ignorant, the righteous and the wicked. And there would be no difference between what benefits people among actions and what corrupts them, what benefits them and what harms them. These polytheists who argue by predestination to abandon what Allah sent His messengers with of His Oneness and faith in Him; if one of them argued with it against another regarding the forfeiture of his rights or the violation of his command, the other would not accept it from him. Rather, these polytheists would blame one another, be hostile to one another, and fight one another over the deed of one who intended to abandon their rights or to wrong them. So when the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, came to them calling them to the right of Allah over His servants and obedience to His command, they argued by predestination; so they came to argue by predestination to abandon the right of their Lord and to violate His command, with what they would not accept from one who abandoned their right and violated their command. In the two Sahihs, from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "O Mu'adh ibn Jabal! Do you know what the right of Allah over His servants is?" He said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "Its right over His servants is that they worship Him and not associate anything with Him. Do you know what the right of the servants over Allah is, if they do that?" He said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "Its right over them is that He not punish them."

The argument from divine decree (*qadar*) is the attitude of the people of *jahiliyyah* (pre-Islamic ignorance), who have no knowledge of what they do or leave undone: ﴿They follow nothing but conjecture, and they are only guessing﴾. They invoke it only to abandon the right of their Lord and to oppose His command, not to abandon what they themselves consider right or to oppose their own commands. For this reason you find that those who invoke and rely on it, from among the ascetics, the Sufis, the poor, the common people, the soldiers, the jurists and others, take refuge in it whenever they follow conjecture and what the souls desire. If they had knowledge and guidance, they would not argue from decree at all. Rather, they rely on it because of the absence of guidance and knowledge. This is a noble principle: whoever attends to it will know the source of error and misguidance for many people.

For this reason you find that the shaykhs and righteous people who uphold the commanding of good and forbidding of evil often enjoin their followers to acquire knowledge of the Law (*shar'*). Often, desires for certain things and love for them arise in them, and they follow their whims in these matters, thinking that it is the religion of God, the Exalted. Yet they have nothing beyond conjecture, taste (*dhawq*) and emotional feeling (*wijdan*), which return to the love of the self and its desire. So they sometimes argue from decree and sometimes from conjecture and guessing, while in reality they are following their whims. But when they follow knowledge, which is what the Lawgiver (*al-Shari'*) ﷺ brought, they depart from conjecture and what the souls desire, and they follow what has come to them from their Lord, which is guidance, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So whoever follows My guidance, he will not go astray nor will he suffer﴾ [Ta-Ha: 123]. God, the Exalted, has mentioned this meaning about the polytheists in the surahs of al-An'am, al-Nahl and al-Zukhruf, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And they say, "If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them." They have no knowledge of that; they are only guessing﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 20]. Thus it is made clear that they have no knowledge of this; they are only guessing. And in the surah of al-An'am He said: ﴿Say, "Then to God belongs the conclusive proof"﴾ [al-An'am: 149], meaning the sending of messengers and the sending down of books, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So that people will have no argument against God after the messengers﴾ [al-Nisa': 165]. Then He affirmed the decree by His saying: ﴿Had He willed, He would have guided you all﴾ [al-An'am: 149]. Thus He established the legal proof (*hujjah shar'iyyah*) and clarified the decreed will (*mashi'ah qadariyyah*), and both are true. And in al-Nahl He said: ﴿Those who associated said, "Had God willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him, neither we nor our fathers, nor would we have prohibited anything besides Him." Likewise did those before them do. So is there upon the messengers except clear notification?﴾ [al-Nahl: 35]. So He, glory be to Him and exalted, made clear that this statement is a denial of the messengers in what they brought, and is not a proof for them. For if it were a proof, it would be invoked to deny every truth and to justify every wrong. Thus in the natural disposition (*fitrah*) of the children of Adam, it is not a valid proof. Rather, whoever argues by it argues for the absence of knowledge and for following conjecture, like the deeds of those who denied the messengers with this objection. The conclusive proof belongs to God through the sending of messengers and the sending down of books, as is established in the authentic hadith from the Prophet ﷺ who said: "No one loves excuse more than God; for this reason He sent messengers as bearers of good news and warners. And no one loves praise more than God; for this reason He praised Himself. And no one is more jealous than God; for this reason He forbade indecencies, whether apparent or hidden."

He made clear that He, glory be to Him, loves praise, and loves to excuse, and hates indecencies. So He loves to be praised for justice and benevolence, and that He not be described as unjust. It is known that whoever lays down for his followers, saying, "Do this and do not do that," and makes this clear to them and removes their excuse, and then they transgress his limits and corrupt their affairs, he has the right to punish them and take vengeance upon them. If they then say, "Did not God decree this upon us? Had God willed, we would not have done this," it is said to them: You have no proof, and you have nothing with which to offer an excuse, and it is clear that what you did was either good or that you were excused in it. Therefore this speech is not acceptable from you.

[p. 3806] The proof has been established against you by what has preceded of clarification and warning. Suppose a ruler (*wali al-amr*) gave a group of people money to deliver to a town, and they traveled with it and left it in the desert where no one was present, and they spent the night far from it. Meanwhile the ruler had sent soldiers to fight some of the enemies, and those soldiers passed along that road, saw that money, and assumed it was a lost find (*luqatah*) that had no owner, so they took it and went away. Then it would be proper for him to punish the first group for their negligence and their failure to guard what he had commanded them to guard. And if they said to him, "You did not inform us that you would send soldiers after us, so that the money could be protected from them!" he would say: This is not obligatory upon me, and had I done it, it would have been an additional favor to you. But it was incumbent upon you to protect it as you protect deposits and trusts. His proof against them remains standing, and he would not be described as an oppressor among them, even if he did not help them by informing them of those soldiers. Rather, he performed what was beneficial in sending both the first and the latter.

God, glory be to Him and exalted, and to Him belongs the highest likeness, is a just Judge in all that He has made, and nothing goes outside His will and power. So when He commands people to guard the limits and to establish the obligations for their benefit, that is from His kindness toward them and making known to them what benefits them. And when He creates other matters, and then they are negligent and transgress because of His creating those other matters, He is just and wise in creating this and creating that, and in commanding this and commanding that. And even if He did not supply the first group with an increase by which they would guard themselves against negligence and aggression, especially with His knowledge that such an increase, had He created it, would have entailed the loss of a greater benefit, for opposites cannot be combined.

The purpose here is that no one argues from decree except as an argument of mere causal justification, to support following the truth that knowledge has made clear. For man is living, sensing, and moved by will. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said: "The truest of names is al-Harith and Hammam." Al-Harith is the one who earns and works, and al-Hammam is the one who is moved by aspiration (*hamm*). Aspiration is the origin of will and intention. So every person is a *harith* and a *hammam*, one who is moved by will, and this does not occur except after sensation and awareness. For will is preceded by awareness of the object willed, so there is no conceiving of will, love, longing, choice, or seeking except after awareness and what is of its kind, such as sensation, knowledge, hearing, sight, smell, taste, touch, and similar things. This perception and awareness is the prerequisite of will, love and seeking. The living being is naturally disposed to love what benefits it and suits it, and to hate what harms it and repels it. When it conceives of the thing that suits it and benefits it, it wills and loves it. And if it conceives of the thing that harms it, it hates it and recoils from it. But that conception may be knowledge, or it may be conjecture and guessing. If he knows that what he wills is beneficial, that it is the good and what suits him, then he is upon guidance and truth. And if he has no knowledge of that, he is following conjecture and what his soul desires. But if knowledge and clarification come to him that this is not a benefit, he begins to argue from decree, an argument of obstinacy and evasion, not an argument of reliance upon truth and knowledge. Thus no one argues from decree, inwardly or outwardly, except for lack of knowledge of what the truth is. And if this is the case, whoever argues from decree against the messengers is acknowledging that he does not have knowledge of what he holds, and that he speaks without knowledge. Whoever speaks without knowledge is false in his speech, and whoever argues without knowledge has a refuted argument. Either he is ignorant, in which case he must follow knowledge; or he has come to know the truth and followed his whim, in which case he must follow the truth and abandon his whim. It is thus made clear that the one who argues from decree is following his whim without knowledge: ﴿And who is more astray than one who follows his whim without guidance from God?﴾ [al-Qasas: 50]. End of quotation. He has a comprehensive continuation that is worth consulting.

Al-Qashani said regarding this verse: They only said that out of obstinacy and stubbornness, from excessive ignorance, and as a challenge to the monotheists, based on their own doctrine. For if they had said it out of knowledge and certainty, they would have been monotheists, not polytheists, by ascribing will and influence to other than God. For whoever knows that nothing can occur without the will of God, knows that if every being in the world willed something, and God did not will it, it could not occur. So he acknowledges the negation of power and will from all besides God, and thus he would not remain a polytheist. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Had God willed, they would not have associated﴾ [al-An'am: 107]. And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So did those before them﴾, i.e., in denying the messengers out of obstinacy. End of quotation.

The Imam, the Mufti of Egypt, said in his tafsir of Surat al-Asr, from this discussion, the following in substance: Reason, the Law, the senses and inner feeling (*wijdan*) all agree that the act of the servant is his act. That all things return to God, the Exalted, and the existence of contingent beings, is merely their attribution to Him. It is not conceivable to consider them existing except when they are considered as dependent upon Him, which is established by proof, and indeed nearly reaches self-evidence in this way. The same is said regarding the greatness of God's power, the Exalted. If He wills, He can strip us of the power and choice that He has granted us. This is a matter we witness every day: we arrange something, then obstacles come to prevent its realization that were not in our reckoning, and we undertake a work, then our power is cut off from completing it. All of this is beyond dispute. The comprehensiveness of God's knowledge of what has been and what will be is established by proof, and there is no doubt about it among the adherents of the religion. Therefore it is obligatory upon the Muslim to believe that God is the Creator of everything in the manner that He knows, and to affirm the attribution of his action to Him as is self-evident to him. He knows what He has commanded him and avoids what He has forbidden him by using that choice which he finds within himself. He is not obliged after this to raise his gaze beyond it. God has censured the polytheists for their saying: ﴿Had God willed, we would not have associated, neither we nor our fathers, nor would we have prohibited anything﴾ [al-An'am: 148]. Traditions have come with meanings in mutual reinforcement (*mutawatir al-ma'na*) forbidding delving into the decree and its secret. If the servant patiently persevered to the utmost patience, he would stop at what God has set for him as limit, and would not incline by himself to transgress the limits of God that He has set for His servants. I do not wish to speak on this question more than this; otherwise I would have left the patient, and plunged into the question of decree with those who plunge. Whoever is seized by confusion and imagines that we must believe the servant has no act, has contradicted the Book of God and disobeyed the Messenger of God. And I may say, and my reliance is upon God in what I say: whoever says that goes outside the religion of God and nullifies the Law of God, so let the believer in God beware of saying that. End of quotation.

In another place he said: Arguing for abandoning action on the basis of decree is among the doctrines of the atheists. The Noble Book has come to denounce their belief and to censure them for it. It has related to us what they used to say, such as: ﴿Had God willed, we would not have associated, neither we nor our fathers, nor would we have prohibited anything﴾ [al-An'am: 148]. It is not permissible for any of us, while claiming to believe in the Qur'an, to argue with what the polytheists used to argue with. End of quotation. And His, the Exalted, saying:
